    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  x_i, x_j = augment(x), augment(x)
  h_i, h_j = f(x_i), f(x_j)  # shared
  z_i, z_j = g(h_i), g(h_j)
  z = normalize(cat([z_i, z_j]))  # 2N
  sim = z @ z.T
  sim.fill_diagonal_(-inf)  # self
  pos = (arange(2N) + N) % 2N
  loss = cross_entropy(sim / tau, pos)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()  # both
# after training: keep f, use h
del g  # head discarded
h = f(x)  # 2,048-d features

    MoCo and MoCo v2

    Pseudocode

    for x in loader:
  x_q, x_k = aug(x), aug(x)
  # f_k initialized from f_q
  q = f_q(x_q)  # N x C
  k = f_k(x_k).detach()
  # queue: C x K keys, past batches
  l_pos = (q * k).sum(1, True)  # N x 1
  l_neg = q @ queue  # N x K
  logits = cat([l_pos, l_neg], 1)
  labels = zeros(N)  # positive at 0
  loss = CE(logits / t, labels)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()  # f_q
  f_k = m * f_k + (1 - m) * f_q
  enqueue(queue, k); dequeue(queue)
# v2: MLP head, blur, cosine lr, t=0.2

    Query and key views

    • crop, color jitter, flip, grayscale (v1)
    • Two random views of one patch; training pulls them together.

    Two encoders

    • query encoder, trained by backpropagation
    • key encoder: no gradients, initialized from f_q
    • The key encoder is a slow, gradient-free copy of the query encoder.

    Normalized embeddings

    • 128 ResNet-50, then fc to 128-d, ℓ2-normalized
    • detached; key batch shuffled across GPUs (shuffling BN)
    • Each view becomes a unit vector: or .

    Dictionary as a queue

    • negatives come from the queue, decoupled from the batch size (256)
    • The dictionary of negatives can be far bigger than the batch.

    InfoNCE over keys

    • the key of the same image, at index 0
    • 0.07 in v1
    • Train to find its own key among .

    Momentum update

    • momentum coefficient, 0.999
    • Slow drift keeps old and new keys in the queue comparable.

    Update the queue

    • queue keys from recent batches by a slowly changing encoder
    • This batch’s keys join; the oldest batch leaves.

    MoCo intuition

    Why a large number of negatives helps

    Many negatives push the model to learn more discriminative, more generalizable representations.

    Imagine training with only 2 negatives

    A pathology foundation model trained with contrastive learning. The query is an H&E patch with tumor cells.

    • Positive another augmented view of the same patch
    • Negative 1 an adipose tissue patch
    • Negative 2 a background tissue patch

    These negatives are easy to tell apart from the query. The model can get by with simple features, without understanding subtler histological differences.

    Now imagine 65,536 negatives

    The queue holds embeddings from many different tissue patches:

    • adipose tissue
    • normal epithelium
    • tumor cells
    • inflammatory cells
    • different tumor morphologies

    Now the model meets hard negatives: patches that look like the query but come from different images, such as two tumor patches with very similar nuclear morphology.

    To tell them apart, the model must learn more detailed features. That is what makes the representation more discriminative.

    More negatives → more hard negatives → finer, more discriminative features

    Barlow Twins

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  y_a, y_b = augment(x), augment(x)
  h_a, h_b = f(y_a), f(y_b)  # shared
  z_a, z_b = g(h_a), g(h_b)  # N x D
  z_a = (z_a - z_a.mean(0)) / z_a.std(0)
  z_b = (z_b - z_b.mean(0)) / z_b.std(0)
  c = z_a.T @ z_b / N  # D x D
  on = ((diag(c) - 1) ** 2).sum()
  off = (off_diagonal(c) ** 2).sum()
  loss = on + lambd * off
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
# after training: keep f, use h

    Two augmented views

    • crop, flip, color jitter, grayscale, blur, solarization
    • independent draws; blur and solarization odds differ per view

    One encoder, shared weights

    • encoder (ResNet-50), the same weights for both views
    • 2,048-d representation kept for downstream tasks

    A wide projector

    • projector: 3 linear layers of 8,192 units
    • BN, ReLU after the first two layers

    Standardize each dimension over the batch

    • mean and standard deviation of dimension over the batch
    • a sample in the batch (2,048 in the paper)

    Cross-correlation between the views

    • , entries between −1 and 1
    • embedding dimensions, not samples

    Barlow Twins loss

    • 5 × 10⁻³, weights the redundancy term
    • invariance: each dimension agrees across views
    • redundancy reduction: dimensions decorrelate

    Target

    • identity matrix
    • no negatives, predictor, stop-gradient or momentum encoder

    VICReg

    Pseudocode

    for x in loader:
  x_a, x_b = augment(x), augment(x)
  y_a, y_b = f(x_a), f(x_b)
  z_a, z_b = h(y_a), h(y_b)  # N x D
  sim = mse_loss(z_a, z_b); v = c = 0
  for z in (z_a, z_b):  # each branch
    std = sqrt(z.var(0) + 1e-4)
    v += relu(1 - std).mean()
  for z in (z_a, z_b):
    C = cov(z)  # D x D
    c += off_diag(C).pow(2).sum() / D
  loss = 25 * sim + 25 * v + 1 * c
  loss.backward(); opt.step()

    Two augmented views

    • the image; and are its two views
    • crop, flip, color jitter, grayscale, blur, solarization

    An encoder per branch

    • encoder (ResNet-50); its 2,048-d output is kept
    • usually equal to , but the branches may differ

    Expander

    • expander: 3 layers of 8,192 units, discarded after training
    • a batch of embeddings, not normalized

    Invariance

    • batch size (2,048 in the paper)
    • the only term that links the two branches
    • Invariance: Pulls two augmented views of the same image closer together.

    Variance (hinge on the std)

    • target standard deviation, 1
    • 10⁻⁴, keeps the square root stable
    • dimension across the batch, per branch
    • Variance: Prevents different images from all being mapped to the same representation.

    Covariance, within each branch

    • covariance within one branch
    • vs. Barlow Barlow Twins correlates the two branches
    • Covariance: Encourages different embedding dimensions to carry nonredundant information.

    Total loss

    • ImageNet defaults
    • no negatives, stop-gradient, predictor or normalization
    • Invariance: Pulls two augmented views of the same image closer together.
    • Variance: Prevents different images from all being mapped to the same representation.
    • Covariance: Encourages different embedding dimensions to carry nonredundant information.

    DINO

    Pseudocode

    # x: unlabeled H&E patch
for x in wsi_patches:
  crops = multi_crop(x)
  v_s = crops  # 2 global + n local
  v_t = crops[:2]  # same globals
  s = student(v_s)
  # teacher: stop gradient
  with no_grad():
    t = teacher(v_t)
  p_s = softmax(s / tau_s)
  # center, then sharpen
  p_t = softmax((t - c) / tau_t)
  # teacher global i vs student view j
  loss = mean(H(p_t[i], p_s[j])
    for i in (0, 1)
    for j in views if j != i)
  loss.backward()
  optimizer.step()  # student
  teacher = ema(teacher, student)
  c = ema(c, t.mean(0))

    • all views of patch
    • 2 global crops, 224 px
    • local crops, 96 px
    • number of local crops

    Teacher views

    • all views the student sees

    Stop gradient

    • teacher weights, never trained by the loss
    • DINO loss

    Student softmax

    • student logit for one view
    • output dimensions, 65,536 in DINO
    • student temperature, 0.1

    Centered, sharpened teacher softmax

    • teacher logit
    • center, a running mean of
    • teacher temperature, warmed up from 0.04 to 0.07, below τₛ

    Cross-entropy across views

    • cross-entropy

    MAE

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  p = patchify(x)  # B x 196 x 768
  keep, mask = random_masking(0.75)
  z = encoder(p[keep] + pos[keep])
  t = cat([z, m.repeat(n_masked)])
  t = unshuffle(t) + pos
  p_hat = decoder(t)
  # p_hat: pixels for all 196 patches
  y = (p - p.mean(-1)) / p.std(-1)
  err = ((p_hat - y) ** 2).mean(-1)
  loss = err[mask].mean()
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
# after: keep encoder, drop decoder

    Patchify

    • one 16 × 16 px patch (7 × 7 of 196 shown)

    Random masking

    • masked patches, sampled uniformly at random

    Encoder on visible patches only

    • ViT encoder (ViT-B/16, L/16, H/14)
    • positional embedding of patch
    • 25% of tokens enter the encoder, so pretraining is cheaper

    Mask tokens join the sequence

    • one shared, learned mask token

    Lightweight decoder

    • decoder: 8 blocks, 512-d, about 9% of ViT-L’s FLOPs per token

    Reconstructed pixels

    • 768 = 16 × 16 × 3 pixel values per patch

    Loss on masked patches

    • mean and std of patch i’s own pixels
    • the loss is computed on masked patches only

    Downstream

    • discarded after pretraining
    • aug. random crop and flip only

    iBOT

    Pseudocode

    # x: unlabeled H&E patch
for x in wsi_patches:
  crops = multi_crop(x)
  m = block_masks(crops[:2])
  v_t = crops[:2]  # unmasked
  f_cls, f_tok = backbone(crops, m)
  s_cls = head(f_cls)  # shared
  s_tok = head(f_tok[m])
  with no_grad():  # teacher
    t_cls, t_tok = teacher(v_t)
  p_s = softmax(s_cls / tau_s)
  q_s = softmax(s_tok / tau_s)
  p_t = softmax((t_cls - c) / tau_t)
  q_t = softmax((t_tok[m] - c2) / tau_t2)
  l_cls = H(p_t, p_s)  # other view
  l_mim = H(q_t, q_s)  # same view
  loss = l_cls + l_mim
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  teacher = ema(teacher, student)
  c, c2 = ema(c, t_cls), ema(c2, t_tok)

    DINOv2

    Pseudocode

    # x: unlabeled H&E patch
for x in wsi_patches:
  crops = multi_crop(x)
  m = random_masks(crops[:2])
  v_t = crops[:2]  # unmasked
  f_cls, f_tok = backbone(crops, m)
  s_cls = dino_head(f_cls)
  s_tok = ibot_head(f_tok[m])
  with no_grad():  # teacher
    t_cls, t_tok = teacher(v_t)
  p_s = softmax(s_cls / tau_s)
  q_s = softmax(s_tok / tau_s)
  p_t = sinkhorn(t_cls / tau_t)
  q_t = sinkhorn(t_tok[m] / tau_t)
  l_dino = H(p_t, p_s)  # other views
  l_ibot = H(q_t, q_s)  # same crop
  l_koleo = koleo(f_cls)  # per view
  loss = l_dino + l_ibot + 0.1 * l_koleo
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  teacher = ema(teacher, student)

    CLIP

    Pseudocode

    # N (image, caption) pairs from the web
for imgs, texts in loader:
  i_e = l2norm(image_enc(imgs) @ W_i)
  t_e = l2norm(text_enc(texts) @ W_t)
  # both: N x d_e, unit length
  logits = exp(t) * i_e @ t_e.T  # N x N
  labels = arange(N)  # diagonal
  loss = (CE(logits, labels)
        + CE(logits.T, labels)) / 2
  loss.backward(); opt.step()
  t.clamp_(max=log(100))
# zero-shot, no training
T = l2norm(text_enc(prompts) @ W_t)
pred = argmax(i_e @ T.T)

    Pseudocode

    # x: images, y: caption token ids
for x, y in loader:
  v = vit(x)  # B x 256 x D
  v_gen = gen_pool(v)  # 256 q
  e_x = con_pool(v_gen)  # 1 q
  h = uni_dec(cat([y, cls]))
  e_y = h[:, -1]  # [CLS]
  l_con = clip_loss(e_x, e_y, sigma)
  z = multi_dec(h[:, :-1], v_gen)
  # next-token prediction
  l_cap = CE(z[:, :-1], y[:, 1:])
  loss = 1.0 * l_con + 2.0 * l_cap
  loss.backward()  # one pass, both
# embeddings: zero-shot, retrieval
# decoder: captions, VQA

    Pseudocode

    # x: N unlabeled H&E patches
for x in loader:
  blocks = sample_targets(4)  # 15-20%
  ctx = sample_context()  # 85-100%
  ctx = ctx - union(blocks)
  s_x = ctx_enc(x, keep=ctx)
  with no_grad():

loss = 0
for b in blocks:
    queries = mask_token + pos_embed[b]
    pred = predictor(s_x, queries)
    loss += l2(pred, s_y[b])
  loss = loss / len(blocks)
  loss.backward(); opt.step()

    # DINOv2 loop; two swaps for tissue
for tiles in loader:
  # before: RandomResizedCrop(224,

    DINOv2 for pathology intuition

    KoLeo vs KDE: why swap the regularizer?

    Both push embeddings apart so tiles don’t collapse to one point. They differ when two embeddings are almost identical.

    KoLeoKDE kernel
    penalty = 0.69 = 4.38
    gradient = −2 = −2.5
    as explodesstays finite, gradient → 0

    von Mises–Fisher (vMF) kernel

    What is vMF?＋
    5
    0 · uniform directions20 · tight concentration

    Dots are illustrative vMF samples on a 3D unit sphere. The arrow marks the preferred direction μ.

    View reference image

    von Mises–Fisher (vMF) naturally models directions on a hypersphere.

    zi⊤zj=cos(θij)

    For normalized embeddings, the dot product measures angular similarity. It depends on the angle between their directions, with each embedding having unit magnitude.

    The von Mises–Fisher distribution describes directions on the unit sphere. A preferred direction sets the center of concentration, and κ controls how tightly points cluster around it.

    For normalized embeddings, the vMF kernel gives higher weight to directions with greater cosine similarity. Increasing κ makes this preference sharper.

    k(zi,zj)=eκzi⊤zj
    zi,zj
    Two normalized image embeddings.
    zi⊤zj
    Cosine similarity.
    κ=5
    Controls how sharply the kernel responds to similarity.

    For unit-normalized embeddings, d2=2−2zi⊤zj. Substituting gives

    k(d)=eκe−κd2/2

    A smooth Gaussian-shaped distance profile, highest at zero and decreasing over 0≤d≤2.

    KDE aggregates the entire batch

    LKDE=1N ∑ilog( ∑j≠i eκzi⊤zj)

    For each embedding, sum the kernel similarities to every other embedding in the batch. Take the logarithm, then average over the N anchors.

    Minimize this loss to discourage excessive concentration of embeddings. It is the negative of the paper’s kernel entropy estimator.

    The distance plot shows one pair’s kernel contribution. The batch loss applies a log to the sum of all contributions for each anchor.

    Why a diversity term at all?

    Invariance: two views of the same tile should match, .

    Diversity: different tiles should not all collapse, . DINO’s own tricks help too; this term adds to them.

    KoLeo’s problem in pathology

    Tissue repeats across patients: two normal liver tiles can look almost the same, so often. The push then explodes and can split tiles that should stay close.

    KDE’s fix: a bounded kernel

    The penalty never exceeds , and its gradient fades to 0 near duplicates. Same goal, stable gradients.

    KoLeo’s push explodes for near-duplicate tiles. KDE’s push stays finite.

    Why use a projection head?

    The MLP separates learning useful features from optimizing the contrastive loss.

    Image x→Encoder f→h→MLP g→z→Contrastive loss

    Representation space h

    The encoder produces a rich representation of morphology, texture, color, and other image features.

    These features can support a range of downstream tasks, including tasks that use information affected by the training augmentations.

    Contrastive space z

    The projection head transforms h into z, where the contrastive loss is applied.

    The loss encourages agreement between augmented views. This can suppress augmentation-specific information, such as stain variations.

    A buffer between the objectives

    Applying the loss to z gives the projector room to specialize in augmentation invariance, while h can preserve additional information useful downstream.

    Gradients still flow through the projector to train the encoder.

    After pretraining

    SimCLR found that representations before the projection head, h, performed better on downstream evaluation. Discard the projector and retain the encoder for downstream use.

    DINO intuition

    Why centering and sharpening?

    With no labels, the student can match the teacher trivially by giving every image the same answer. Each operation blocks one way of collapsing.

    Collapse: every output is flatCollapse: one dimension wins for every patchHealthy: confident and different per patch

    Patch 1
    Patch 2
    Patch 3
    avgBatch average

    teacher output over dimensions = 1 … 8

    Centering: subtract a running mean

    is the average teacher output over recent batches. Subtracting it means no single dimension can win for every image.

    On its own, centering pushes the teacher toward a flat, uniform output. A flat target tells the student nothing.

    Sharpening: a lower teacher temperature

    Dividing by a small makes the teacher’s softmax peaked and confident, sharper than the student’s ().

    On its own, sharpening lets one dimension win for every image, so every image looks the same.

    Together: confident and diverse

    Centering keeps the dimensions balanced across the batch. Sharpening keeps each image’s target confident.

    The two pull in opposite directions, so the teacher can’t settle into either collapse.

    Each patch gets its own clear target, so the student has something real to learn.

    Centering stops one dimension from dominating. Sharpening stops the output from going flat. You need both.
